Rockstar Games fired me on Wednesday. GTA 6 launched on Thursday.

I was a Senior Engine Engineer at Rockstar North, working on RAGE infrastructure and internal tooling. I've been with the studio for six years. I shipped RDR2 on PC. I was part of the core team for GTA 6 since pre-production.

What I'm about to tell you is not about me getting fired. It's about something that every game studio, every tech company, and every software corporation on earth is about to face and none of them are ready for it.

Their entire business model is about to collapse. And I have the proof because I accidentally did it on a Saturday afternoon.

In August I started experimenting with AI agent workflows. Not on company time. Not on company hardware. On my personal laptop, on a weekend. I wanted to see what would happen if I described one of our internal tools to an AI the way I would explain it to a new hire.

I opened Claude Code running Fable 5.2. I described our mission scripting pipeline. Not from documentation. Not from source code. From memory. The way any senior engineer talks about systems they built - the architecture, the data flow, the edge cases, the design decisions.

The AI asked me follow-up questions. I answered them the way I'd answer a junior developer during onboarding. Normal engineering conversation. The kind that happens in every standup, every code review, every lunch break at every tech company in the world.

Then it started building.

Eleven hours later I had a functionally complete recreation of a system that took our team fourteen months to ship.

I need you to understand what "functionally complete" means. This is not a rough sketch. This is not a prototype. The state machine was correct. The event pipeline worked. The edge cases were handled. The build compiled. It ran. I tested it against real scenarios from memory. It passed every single one.

Fourteen months of work by a team of engineers. Rebuilt from a conversation. In eleven hours. By one person who wasn't even trying that hard.

But that's not the part that should scare you. Here's the part that should scare you.

I didn't do anything that any engineer at any company couldn't do right now.

I didn't hack into Rockstar's servers. I didn't export a single file. I didn't copy a single line of source code. I didn't use any company credentials. I didn't access any internal repository. I didn't violate any access controls. I didn't even open my work laptop.

I talked to an AI about how software works. That's it. That's the whole crime.

Every engineer reading this has done a version of what I did. Every time you've described your company's architecture to ChatGPT to debug a problem. Every time you've explained a system design to Claude to get a second opinion. Every time you've pasted a stack trace and described the surrounding code to Copilot.

You've been doing what I did. The only difference is you didn't compile the output.

I compiled it. And it worked. And that's when everything went wrong.

I brought the prototype to my technical lead on Monday. I was excited. I thought I had discovered something that could save the studio thousands of engineering hours. I thought this was the future of how we build tools. I thought they'd promote me.

He went quiet. He asked me to send him the files. I did.

48 hours later I was in a room with Legal, HR, and my department head. No technical leads in the room. No engineers. No one who would understand what I actually did. Just lawyers.

They told me I had "reproduced proprietary systems and internal tools outside of the approved development environment using unauthorized AI agent workflows." They told me the resulting build was "functionally complete" and represented a "material breach of our Security and Intellectual Property policies."

Then they told me the number.

$47,500,000.

Forty-seven point five million dollars in estimated damages. For a conversation I had with an AI on my personal laptop on a Saturday.

They presented me with a termination letter. Effective immediately. They had already revoked my access across every Rockstar system before I walked into that room. Badge. Email. VPN. Jira. Confluence. Perforce. Six years - gone before I sat down in the chair.

The letter says they've referred the matter to external counsel. It says they're cooperating with federal authorities. It says I need to return all company hardware and removable media by Monday.

I want to be very clear about what's actually happening here because the framing in that letter is designed to make me look like a spy. Like I broke into a vault and walked out with the blueprints.

Here's what actually happened: I described how software works to a machine that understands software. And the machine built it.

That's it. That's the $47.5 million crime.

And here's why Rockstar is terrified. Here's why they went straight to lawyers instead of engineers. Here's why the number is $47.5 million instead of a written warning.

Because if what I did works - and it does work, I have the build to prove it - then the fundamental premise of the entire software industry is broken.

Every company in tech operates on one core assumption: our code is our moat. Our proprietary systems are our competitive advantage. It took us years to build this, and that time investment is what protects us.

I just proved that assumption is wrong.

The moat is not the code. The code can be rebuilt in eleven hours. The moat is not the architecture. The architecture lives in the heads of the engineers. The moat is not the years of investment. The years of investment can be compressed into a single conversation.

The only moat left is the people. And the people can talk.

Not to competitors. Not to journalists. Not to foreign governments. To AI. To a tool that anyone can download and run on a laptop.

Rockstar's $47.5 million is not about punishing me. It's about sending a message to every engineer in that building: do not talk to AI about what you know. Do not describe your work. Do not explain your systems. Because if you do, those systems can be rebuilt overnight. And we will end you.

That's not a security policy. That's a gag order on human knowledge.

Here's the part that keeps me up at night.

I did this by accident. I wasn't trying to steal anything. I wasn't trying to prove a point. I was running a weekend experiment. What happens when someone actually tries? What happens when a competitor hires three senior engineers from a game studio and sits them down with an AI for a week? What happens when every startup in the world realizes they don't need to build from scratch - they just need to hire people who've built before?

This is already happening. It's happening right now. And the only reason you haven't heard about it is because everyone who discovers it gets a termination letter and a threat before they can tell anyone.

I'm telling you.

This is the termination email. I've redacted my name and personal details.

$47.5 million. For talking to Claude.

hits.full_text:
This is f**king wild. Google paid $40 million for Fossil's smartwatch tech and $2.1 billion for Fitbit. One developer took a $40 board and got a Pixel Watch-style interface running at 60 FPS in two evenings with Claude Code:

"I vibe coded for two days, two evenings, and got a great interface."

The board is a Waveshare ESP32-S3, an Espressif chip, with a round 466x466 AMOLED screen and no GPU. On the factory firmware the icons tear into pieces when you scroll, and you can't even drag them with your finger.

He dropped the vendor's libraries. No LVGL, no Arduino_GFX. With Claude Code, Anthropic's coding agent, he wrote his own display driver, touch driver and drawing library from scratch. Then Claude Opus 5.5 ported Google's open Wear OS samples into it: rolling digits, a Pixel Watch card gallery, weather, a music player.

60 frames per second, zero dropped frames, no tearing. When nothing moves it draws zero frames. He says it feels close to an Apple Watch or an iPhone.

At 3:22 the stock firmware's icons tear apart mid-scroll. At 4:16 his first try on the standard driver strobes.

The part that got me is what he says about the companies behind these boards: they write the drivers and still can't ship a decent interface. He did it in two evenings with Opus 5.5. Now imagine it on Claude Fable 5.2.

It's open source on GitHub, and you flash it from Chrome in a couple of minutes.

Would you wear a $40 watch you built with Claude?

This is BEYOND insane:

A TOOTHPASTE COMPANY JUST SHOWED AI CAN PREDICT WHAT CUSTOMERS WILL BUY.

Colgate's researchers tested it against 57 real product surveys and 9,300 real people.

The AI got close to how consistent humans are with themselves.

Here's the trick.

If you ask an AI "rate this product from 1 to 5," it gives you safe, middle of the road answers. Useless.

They gave the AI a customer profile. Age. Income. Background.

Showed it a product.

Then a second model turned those thoughts into a score.

The results:

→ about 90% of human test retest reliability
→ realistic differences across age and income groups
→ written feedback that was more detailed than most real survey answers

Market research usually takes weeks and costs thousands.

This runs overnight.

It won't replace talking to real customers.

But it changes how fast you can test an idea before you do.

This is f**king wild. Google paid $40 million for Fossil's smartwatch tech and $2.1 billion for Fitbit. One developer took a $40 board and got a Pixel Watch-style interface running at 60 FPS in two evenings with Claude Code:

"I vibe coded for two days, two evenings, and got a great interface."

The board is a Waveshare ESP32-S3, an Espressif chip, with a round 466x466 AMOLED screen and no GPU. On the factory firmware the icons tear into pieces when you scroll, and you can't even drag them with your finger.

He dropped the vendor's libraries. No LVGL, no Arduino_GFX. With Claude Code, Anthropic's coding agent, he wrote his own display driver, touch driver and drawing library from scratch. Then Claude Opus 5.5 ported Google's open Wear OS samples into it: rolling digits, a Pixel Watch card gallery, weather, a music player.

60 frames per second, zero dropped frames, no tearing. When nothing moves it draws zero frames. He says it feels close to an Apple Watch or an iPhone.

At 3:22 the stock firmware's icons tear apart mid-scroll. At 4:16 his first try on the standard driver strobes.

The part that got me is what he says about the companies behind these boards: they write the drivers and still can't ship a decent interface. He did it in two evenings with Opus 5.5. Now imagine it on Claude Fable 5.2.

It's open source on GitHub, and you flash it from Chrome in a couple of minutes.

Would you wear a $40 watch you built with Claude?

Video: PopaSpinka on YouTube

This is f*cking insane... uncensored Claude Code is porting GTA VI to PC

no emulator, no console. Just a GitHub repo that ports PS5 executables straight to Windows

here's what my uncensored Claude did, step by step:

step 1 → relinked the PS5 build into a format Windows can load

step 2 → audited every system call the game makes and swapped in replacements for the PS5 libraries

the tool behind it → https://t.co/XRvLcPrW9a
→ ports PS5 executables to Windows and Linux automatically
→ no emulation. It rebuilds the game as a native PC program. PS5 and PC share the same x86-64 CPU, so the code runs directly
→ ships its own versions of the PS5 system libraries, so the game thinks it's still on a console
→ built-in shader converter: PS5 shaders → SPIR-V for Vulkan
→ open source, GPL-2.0, C++. 59k stars, 47k+ commits, updated daily, dozens co-authored by Claude
→ doesn't crack or decrypt anything. You feed it a game file you already own

step 3 → translated the console's graphics commands and shaders into Vulkan, thousands of them

step 4 → launched it. Crashed. Read the log, patched the fault, reran. Over and over until it held

step 5 → measured real gameplay, not the menu. A build can boot fine and still die when the world loads

where it's at right now: it boots, it drives, ~28 FPS. Port still in progress, updates coming

my uncensored LLM setup is in the comments. Save this before everyone's doing it

posts.full_text:
IF YOU'RE STILL BABYSITTING YOUR AI AGENT, THE PROBLEM ISN'T THE AGENT. IT'S YOU.

Matt Pocock just shipped a 21,000 line feature without hovering over every step.

Then he wrote down exactly how in a 10 page PDF.

His skills repo reportedly has more stars than React.

Here's the formula:

Feature = Codebase + Grill + Spec + Tickets + AFK Loop + Retro

Most people hand the agent the "what" and then micromanage every step of the "how."

He does the opposite.

The 10 layers:

0. Codebase: deep modules and fast feedback. Bad codebases make bad agents.
1. Setup: tell the skills how your repo works, once.
2. Grill: the agent interviews you until every question is answered. Give it the why.
3. Glossary: one word per idea. The reasons go in decision records.
4. Prototype: 3 throwaway versions. Keep the decision, not the code.
5. Spec to tickets: small vertical slices, each one demoable.
6. AFK loop: the agent grabs the next ticket, writes tests first, commits, repeats overnight.
7. Review: a fresh reviewer checks your standards before you even look.
8. Stack and QA: humans only review the decisions you can't undo.
9. Retro: every review comment becomes a lint rule.

The result:

47 user stories.
9 parallel tickets.
About 21,000 lines.
All 12 review comments turned into permanent rules.

Here's my take.

Most developers complaining that AI writes bad code never gave it a good codebase, a clear spec or a single rule.

Then they blame the model.

The agent was never the bottleneck.

The process was.

MICROSOFT DIDN'T KILL BACKPROPAGATION. THEY DID SOMETHING MORE UNCOMFORTABLE.

They proved we don't always need black boxes.

Researchers had an AI agent, reportedly Claude Opus 5.5, write a neural network's weights by hand.

In Python.

No gradient descent. No training run. No pretrained weights.

The agent writes a hypothesis directly into the weights.

Tests it.

Reads the score.

Rewrites it.

Like a scientist, not a GPU farm.

Then they pointed it at the human brain.

On visual brain scans, it beat every existing interpretable model.

On auditory recordings, it found sound features that predict brain activity.

And on language brain scans, something wild happened.

The score suddenly jumped.

With a black box, that's a paper.

Because this one writes readable code, they looked inside.

The AI was cheating. It was exploiting a flaw in the scan data, not understanding language.

They caught it only because they could read it.

Here's my take.

The AI industry is addicted to bigger.

Bigger models. Bigger clusters. Bigger black boxes.

And nobody can explain what's happening inside any of them.

This paper is a quiet warning.

How many "breakthroughs" out there are just models cheating in ways nobody can see?

A CFO runs the monthly close on Fable 5.2 for $90 a month and catches what a $250,000 audit firm samples right past. Five agents and one rule about which numbers are allowed to move.

She shared the whole playbook.

Her version starts from the opposite idea. Closing the books is not about adding things up. It's about proving nothing changed without a reason.

Five agents. Every entry carries the document that justifies it:

> MATCH - pairs every bank line with an invoice or receipt
> QUESTION - writes to whoever owns an unmatched line. Waits for proof
> ACCRUE - books what was used but not billed yet
> COMPARE - checks each account against the last twelve closes
> LOCK - seals the period, and a late entry reopens only what it touches

Four agents work the numbers. One decides what is allowed to change after close. A late invoice reopens the three accounts it lands on and leaves the rest sealed.

That's the entire design. A close that can't explain its own edits has to be audited line by line or taken on faith.

She replayed a full year. 61,000 transactions, 214 that moved after close with no document attached. Last year's audit sampled 9 of them.

Everyone else automates the typing. She automated the paper trail. The savings show up the week the auditors arrive.

posts.full_text:
Anthropic built a working model of the ribosome and the first thing it explained was why an antibiotic that saves your life can also take your hearing.

It was not built to design a new drug. It was built to show, atom by atom, where a bacterial ribosome differs from every ribosome inside a human cell.

> COLLECT - 2,600 published structures, bacterial and human, in one format
> BUILD - one moving model that assembles, reads and releases like the real thing
> ALIGN - drug binding sites of both laid on top of each other
> SPLIT - the human copies hiding inside mitochondria pulled out
> KEEP - only pockets that exist in bacteria and nowhere in us

The main human ribosome was never the problem. It looks different enough that most antibiotics slide right past it.

The trouble sits inside mitochondria. Their ribosomes descend from bacteria, and in the inner ear that resemblance is what costs people their hearing.

14 pockets survived the filter. Each one exists in bacteria and has no twin anywhere in a human cell.

A drug that kills bacteria is not a drug that only kills bacteria. The second part was rarely the first thing anyone screened for.

Bacterial and mitochondrial structures sit in different databases, solved by different labs for different reasons. Almost nobody had laid them side by side.

The model in the video is that comparison running live, a drug sliding into a bacterial ribosome and finding nothing to grip in ours.

All 14 pockets are mapped in the article below.

posts.full_text:
4 FREE repos and Claude Fable 5.2 turn a GTA 6 heist into a replay lab... every run gets heard, mapped and compared until one bus makes it out

4 repos, 69K stars, one job each:

listen

1. whisperX (25.6K) - every line of the getaway with word-level timestamps

2. pyannote-audio (10.8K) - tells the voices apart, SPEAKER 0 and SPEAKER 1

map

3. networkx (17.4K) - turns every run into a branch map of outcomes

cut

4. moviepy (15.2K) - cuts the run that worked to 9:16, captions on

Claude Fable 5.2 sits on top: it compares the runs and marks the exact line where each one split

the shift: you stop replaying a mission blind. every run leaves a map (visualization)
